title: The Redeemer Shall Come to Zion

chapters.title: Isaiah 58
chapters.focus: Fasting, helping people in need, and finding joy in the Sabbath.

sources.title: Henry B. Eyring: Is Not This the Fast That I Have Chosen? (April 2015)
Russell M. Nelson: The Sabbath Is a Delight (April 2015)

segments.text: This is a personal study reading of Isaiah chapter fifty-eight for the October twelfth through eighteenth Come Follow Me lesson. Isaiah was a prophet in ancient Israel. The scripture voice will read every verse, and a second voice will pause to explain. The explanations are generated study commentary, with help from sources linked in the lesson.

verses.text: Cry aloud, spare not, lift up thy voice like a trumpet, and shew my people their transgression, and the house of Jacob their sins.

Yet they seek me daily, and delight to know my ways, as a nation that did righteousness, and forsook not the ordinance of their God: they ask of me the ordinances of justice; they take delight in approaching to God.

segments.text: The house of Jacob means Jacob's descendants, the people of Israel. Transgression means wrongdoing. These opening verses describe people who look eager to worship: they seek God and ask to know His ways. Yet Isaiah is told to point out their sins. The question is whether their everyday choices match their religious practices. Listen next for the specific problem God identifies.

verses.text: Wherefore have we fasted, say they, and thou seest not? wherefore have we afflicted our soul, and thou takest no knowledge? Behold, in the day of your fast ye find pleasure, and exact all your labours.
Behold, ye fast for strife and debate, and to smite with the fist of wickedness: ye shall not fast as ye do this day, to make your voice to be heard on high.

Is it such a fast that I have chosen? a day for a man to afflict his soul? is it to bow down his head as a bulrush, and to spread sackcloth and ashes under him? wilt thou call this a fast, and an acceptable day to the Lord?

segments.text: Fasting means voluntarily going without food for a religious purpose. These people wonder why God has not noticed their fasting. But they are still fighting and treating other people harshly. Bowing the head, wearing sackcloth, and sitting in ashes were outward signs of sorrow or humility. God asks them to look beyond those visible actions. What should change in the way they treat others?

verses.text: Is not this the fast that I have chosen? to loose the bands of wickedness, to undo the heavy burdens, and to let the oppressed go free, and that ye break every yoke?

Is it not to deal thy bread to the hungry, and that thou bring the poor that are cast out to thy house? when thou seest the naked, that thou cover him; and that thou hide not thyself from thine own flesh?

segments.text: A yoke is a wooden beam used with animals pulling a load. Here it helps us picture oppression and heavy burdens. The next verse turns that picture into practical help: feed someone hungry, shelter someone without a home, and care for your own people. In the talk linked by the lesson, President Henry B Eyring explains how fast offerings, donations to help people in need, put this care into action. He describes a woman in Sierra Leone who received much-needed clothing and a blanket during wartime, and later gave a small offering herself to help others. Her experience makes Isaiah's words about food and clothing concrete.

verses.text: Then shall thy light break forth as the morning, and thine health shall spring forth speedily: and thy righteousness shall go before thee; the glory of the Lord shall be thy rearward.
Then shalt thou call, and the Lord shall answer; thou shalt cry, and he shall say, Here I am. If thou take away from the midst of thee the yoke, the putting forth of the finger, and speaking vanity;
And if thou draw out thy soul to the hungry, and satisfy the afflicted soul; then shall thy light rise in obscurity, and thy darkness be as the noonday:
And the Lord shall guide thee continually, and satisfy thy soul in drought, and make fat thy bones: and thou shalt be like a watered garden, and like a spring of water, whose waters fail not.

And they that shall be of thee shall build the old waste places: thou shalt raise up the foundations of many generations; and thou shalt be called, The repairer of the breach, The restorer of paths to dwell in.

segments.text: Rearward means a guard behind you. Isaiah pictures God's care surrounding His people. A watered garden and a spring that keeps flowing are images of life and renewal, especially in a dry place. A breach is a gap or break. Repairing breaches and rebuilding ruined places suggest restoring a community where people can live safely. Notice the connection across these verses: helping someone who is struggling goes together with turning toward God.

verses.text: If thou turn away thy foot from the sabbath, from doing thy pleasure on my holy day; and call the sabbath a delight, the holy of the Lord, honourable; and shalt honour him, not doing thine own ways, nor finding thine own pleasure, nor speaking thine own words:

Then shalt thou delight thyself in the Lord; and I will cause thee to ride upon the high places of the earth, and feed thee with the heritage of Jacob thy father: for the mouth of the Lord hath spoken it.

segments.text: The Sabbath is a day set apart for worship and rest. Latter-day Saints observe it on Sunday. Isaiah invites us to find joy in honoring the Lord. In the other talk linked by this lesson, Russell M Nelson explains that Sabbath choices can express our relationship with Heavenly Father. He describes rest and spiritual renewal, strengthening family relationships, and serving people who are lonely or in need. A useful question is: what could I choose this Sunday that helps me draw closer to God or show love to someone? That completes all fourteen verses of Isaiah fifty-eight.

Chapter summary. Isaiah fifty-eight connects worship with the way we treat other people. It begins with a warning: people can go through religious practices while continuing to hurt others. It then describes the fast God desires: freeing people from burdens and meeting practical needs. The chapter closes by inviting us to honor the Sabbath and find joy in the Lord. Here are four lessons to take with you. First, let your worship change your daily actions. Prayer and fasting should help you become kinder. Second, notice people who need help. Sharing food, offering support, and caring for your own family can put faith into action. Third, seek God's guidance as you serve. Isaiah's pictures of light and a watered garden help us imagine the care and renewal God offers. Fourth, make room for God on the Sabbath. Choose time for worship, rest, and loving service. For this week, choose one small action: help someone with a burden, or plan something that helps you find joy in the Sabbath.

chapters.title: Isaiah 59
chapters.focus: Jesus Christ as Savior, Intercessor, and Redeemer

segments.text: This study reading covers Isaiah chapter fifty-nine, with generated explanations for beginners. The chapter describes a community damaged by wrongdoing, then points toward the Lord's power to rescue and redeem.

verses.text: Behold, the Lord’s hand is not shortened, that it cannot save; neither his ear heavy, that it cannot hear:
But your iniquities have separated between you and your God, and your sins have hid his face from you, that he will not hear.
For your hands are defiled with blood, and your fingers with iniquity; your lips have spoken lies, your tongue hath muttered perverseness.
None calleth for justice, nor any pleadeth for truth: they trust in vanity, and speak lies; they conceive mischief, and bring forth iniquity.

segments.text: Iniquity means wrongdoing. Isaiah begins by saying that God still has power to save and hear. He then describes a community where violence, lies, and unfairness have damaged people's relationship with Him. Notice how many examples concern the way people treat one another. The chapter asks us to take honesty and justice seriously as part of our relationship with God.

verses.text: They hatch cockatrice’ eggs, and weave the spider’s web: he that eateth of their eggs dieth, and that which is crushed breaketh out into a viper.
Their webs shall not become garments, neither shall they cover themselves with their works: their works are works of iniquity, and the act of violence is in their hands.
Their feet run to evil, and they make haste to shed innocent blood: their thoughts are thoughts of iniquity; wasting and destruction are in their paths.
The way of peace they know not; and there is no judgment in their goings: they have made them crooked paths: whosoever goeth therein shall not know peace.

segments.text: A cockatrice is a dangerous snake in this old translation. Its eggs picture something harmful being produced and spread. A spider's web looks woven, but it cannot serve as useful clothing. These images help explain the results of wrongdoing: it can spread harm and fail to give lasting protection. Crooked paths describe a way of life that leads people away from peace.

verses.text: Therefore is judgment far from us, neither doth justice overtake us: we wait for light, but behold obscurity; for brightness, but we walk in darkness.
We grope for the wall like the blind, and we grope as if we had no eyes: we stumble at noonday as in the night; we are in desolate places as dead men.
We roar all like bears, and mourn sore like doves: we look for judgment, but there is none; for salvation, but it is far off from us.
For our transgressions are multiplied before thee, and our sins testify against us: for our transgressions are with us; and as for our iniquities, we know them;
In transgressing and lying against the Lord, and departing away from our God, speaking oppression and revolt, conceiving and uttering from the heart words of falsehood.
And judgment is turned away backward, and justice standeth afar off: for truth is fallen in the street, and equity cannot enter.
Yea, truth faileth; and he that departeth from evil maketh himself a prey: and the Lord saw it, and it displeased him that there was no judgment.

segments.text: The speaker now says we and our, admitting the community's problems. Groping in darkness pictures people who cannot find a clear way forward. Equity means fairness. When truth falls in the street, honesty and fairness have lost their place in public life. Even someone who tries to leave evil becomes a target. The people's confession leads into the next question: who will come to help?

verses.text: And he saw that there was no man, and wondered that there was no intercessor: therefore his arm brought salvation unto him; and his righteousness, it sustained him.
For he put on righteousness as a breastplate, and an helmet of salvation upon his head; and he put on the garments of vengeance for clothing, and was clad with zeal as a cloak.
According to their deeds, accordingly he will repay, fury to his adversaries, recompence to his enemies; to the islands he will repay recompence.

So shall they fear the name of the Lord from the west, and his glory from the rising of the sun. When the enemy shall come in like a flood, the Spirit of the Lord shall lift up a standard against him.

segments.text: An intercessor is someone who steps in to help others. The Lord sees that nobody is providing the needed rescue, so He acts with His own power. His arm represents strength; the armor pictures righteousness and salvation. The lesson's Scripture Helps connects this role with Jesus Christ, who brings mercy and stands as our Mediator. The warrior image expresses God's resolve to confront evil and save His people.

verses.text: And the Redeemer shall come to Zion, and unto them that turn from transgression in Jacob, saith the Lord.

As for me, this is my covenant with them, saith the Lord; My spirit that is upon thee, and my words which I have put in thy mouth, shall not depart out of thy mouth, nor out of the mouth of thy seed, nor out of the mouth of thy seed’s seed, saith the Lord, from henceforth and for ever.

segments.text: A redeemer rescues or frees someone. Verse twenty joins the Redeemer's coming with people turning away from transgression, or sin. Zion is the community God is rescuing. Seed means descendants in verse twenty-one. The promise reaches beyond one generation: God's Spirit and His words are to remain among His people and their children. The chapter moves from admitting wrongdoing toward a future shaped by God's help.

Chapter summary. Isaiah fifty-nine begins with injustice and separation from God. The people acknowledge that their actions have produced darkness and suffering. The Lord then steps forward as the powerful rescuer, and the chapter ends with redemption and a covenant promise. Here are four takeaways. First, worship belongs with honesty and fair treatment of others. Second, acknowledging a wrong is an important step toward changing it. Third, look to Jesus Christ as the Redeemer who can help you turn toward God. Fourth, let God's words shape your life and the influence you have on others. One small application is to repair a dishonest or unkind choice: tell the truth, offer an apology, or stand beside someone being treated unfairly. Let that action be part of turning toward the Lord.

chapters.title: Isaiah 60
chapters.focus: The Lord's light and the gathering of His people

sources.title: Bonnie H. Cordon: That They May See (April 2020)

segments.text: This study reading covers Isaiah chapter sixty, with generated explanations for beginners. Isaiah pictures Zion emerging from darkness into God's light, with people gathering from many nations.

verses.text: Arise, shine; for thy light is come, and the glory of the Lord is risen upon thee.
For, behold, the darkness shall cover the earth, and gross darkness the people: but the Lord shall arise upon thee, and his glory shall be seen upon thee.
And the Gentiles shall come to thy light, and kings to the brightness of thy rising.
Lift up thine eyes round about, and see: all they gather themselves together, they come to thee: thy sons shall come from far, and thy daughters shall be nursed at thy side.
Then thou shalt see, and flow together, and thine heart shall fear, and be enlarged; because the abundance of the sea shall be converted unto thee, the forces of the Gentiles shall come unto thee.

segments.text: Isaiah speaks to Zion as though the city were a person. Zion here is associated with Jerusalem and God's people. Light pictures God's presence and guidance; darkness pictures the world's need for that guidance. Gentiles here are people from other nations. The returning sons and daughters picture a scattered family being brought together. Notice that the light draws people toward the Lord.

verses.text: The multitude of camels shall cover thee, the dromedaries of Midian and Ephah; all they from Sheba shall come: they shall bring gold and incense; and they shall shew forth the praises of the Lord.

All the flocks of Kedar shall be gathered together unto thee, the rams of Nebaioth shall minister unto thee: they shall come up with acceptance on mine altar, and I will glorify the house of my glory.
Who are these that fly as a cloud, and as the doves to their windows?

Surely the isles shall wait for me, and the ships of Tarshish first, to bring thy sons from far, their silver and their gold with them, unto the name of the Lord thy God, and to the Holy One of Israel, because he hath glorified thee.

segments.text: Dromedaries are camels. Caravans, ships, flocks, gold, and incense show people coming from far away with things they value. Isaiah's picture is larger than a single city becoming wealthy: the gifts are brought to honor the Lord, and scattered children are brought home. The unusual place names help us imagine many regions participating in this gathering.

verses.text: And the sons of strangers shall build up thy walls, and their kings shall minister unto thee: for in my wrath I smote thee, but in my favour have I had mercy on thee.
Therefore thy gates shall be open continually; they shall not be shut day nor night; that men may bring unto thee the forces of the Gentiles, and that their kings may be brought.
For the nation and kingdom that will not serve thee shall perish; yea, those nations shall be utterly wasted.
The glory of Lebanon shall come unto thee, the fir tree, the pine tree, and the box together, to beautify the place of my sanctuary; and I will make the place of my feet glorious.

The sons also of them that afflicted thee shall come bending unto thee; and all they that despised thee shall bow themselves down at the soles of thy feet; and they shall call thee, The city of the Lord, The Zion of the Holy One of Israel.

segments.text: The open gates and rebuilt walls picture a city restored after suffering. Former enemies now recognize the Lord's city. A sanctuary is a holy place of worship. Isaiah describes a change from humiliation toward honor and safety. The strong warning to opposing nations also shows that God's peace comes with His judgment against resistance and evil.

verses.text: Whereas thou hast been forsaken and hated, so that no man went through thee, I will make thee an eternal excellency, a joy of many generations.
Thou shalt also suck the milk of the Gentiles, and shalt suck the breast of kings: and thou shalt know that I the Lord am thy Saviour and thy Redeemer, the mighty One of Jacob.
For brass I will bring gold, and for iron I will bring silver, and for wood brass, and for stones iron: I will also make thy officers peace, and thine exactors righteousness.
Violence shall no more be heard in thy land, wasting nor destruction within thy borders; but thou shalt call thy walls Salvation, and thy gates Praise.

segments.text: The pictures of milk and nourishment describe support and care. Brass replaced by gold and iron replaced by silver picture an improvement in the people's circumstances. But notice the greatest improvements: peace, righteousness, and the end of violence. Salvation and praise become the names of the walls and gates. Isaiah is helping us imagine what a community under God's care can become.

verses.text: The sun shall be no more thy light by day; neither for brightness shall the moon give light unto thee: but the Lord shall be unto thee an everlasting light, and thy God thy glory.
Thy sun shall no more go down; neither shall thy moon withdraw itself: for the Lord shall be thine everlasting light, and the days of thy mourning shall be ended.
Thy people also shall be all righteous: they shall inherit the land for ever, the branch of my planting, the work of my hands, that I may be glorified.
A little one shall become a thousand, and a small one a strong nation: I the Lord will hasten it in his time.

segments.text: God Himself becomes the lasting source of light. The lesson's Scripture Helps describes both Israel's restoration and a future Zion of peace. We can also think about how we share the Savior's light now. In the linked message, Bonnie H Cordon recalls learning to aim a flashlight at another person's path. Her example invites us to make our help useful to the person receiving it, guiding them toward Christ with thoughtful care.

Chapter summary. Isaiah sixty pictures God's people rising into His light, gathering from far away, and finding restoration. Nations bring gifts, broken places are rebuilt, and violence gives way to peace. The chapter ends with the Lord as an everlasting light. Here are four takeaways. First, seek the guidance God gives when life feels confusing. Second, make room for people who are coming toward Him. Third, measure a thriving community by its peace, fairness, and care for people. Fourth, share light in a way that actually helps someone. A small application might be welcoming a new person, explaining something patiently, or helping someone take a manageable next step. Isaiah's large picture of gathering can help us notice the people within reach of our own kindness.

chapters.title: Isaiah 61
chapters.focus: The Savior's mission to heal, free, and comfort

segments.text: This study reading covers Isaiah chapter sixty-one, with generated explanations for beginners. Its opening words help us recognize the mission of Jesus Christ and the hope He brings to people who are hurting.

verses.text: The Spirit of the Lord God is upon me; because the Lord hath anointed me to preach good tidings unto the meek; he hath sent me to bind up the brokenhearted, to proclaim liberty to the captives, and the opening of the prison to them that are bound;
To proclaim the acceptable year of the Lord, and the day of vengeance of our God; to comfort all that mourn;

To appoint unto them that mourn in Zion, to give unto them beauty for ashes, the oil of joy for mourning, the garment of praise for the spirit of heaviness; that they might be called trees of righteousness, the planting of the Lord, that he might be glorified.

segments.text: Anointed means chosen and set apart for a sacred mission. Good tidings means good news. Luke chapter four records Jesus reading these words and announcing their fulfillment in Him. Binding up a broken heart pictures healing and care. Ashes were a sign of grief; beauty, joyful oil, and a garment of praise picture sorrow being changed. The acceptable year also recalls Jubilee, when ancient Israel was instructed to release burdens and restore freedom.

verses.text: And they shall build the old wastes, they shall raise up the former desolations, and they shall repair the waste cities, the desolations of many generations.
And strangers shall stand and feed your flocks, and the sons of the alien shall be your plowmen and your vinedressers.
But ye shall be named the Priests of the Lord: men shall call you the Ministers of our God: ye shall eat the riches of the Gentiles, and in their glory shall ye boast yourselves.

segments.text: Wastes and desolations mean ruined places. The picture widens from healing individuals to rebuilding a community that has suffered for generations. Strangers and people from other nations participate in its restoration. Ministers means people who serve. The new calling of God's people gives them a responsibility to worship and serve Him as their community is renewed.

verses.text: For your shame ye shall have double; and for confusion they shall rejoice in their portion: therefore in their land they shall possess the double: everlasting joy shall be unto them.
For I the Lord love judgment, I hate robbery for burnt offering; and I will direct their work in truth, and I will make an everlasting covenant with them.
And their seed shall be known among the Gentiles, and their offspring among the people: all that see them shall acknowledge them, that they are the seed which the Lord hath blessed.

segments.text: An everlasting covenant is a lasting sacred relationship with God and His promises. Notice the Lord's character: He loves justice and rejects robbery even when someone uses it to provide a religious offering. Faithful worship should go together with fair actions. Seed and offspring mean descendants. The promised blessings reach families and future generations, replacing the community's shame with renewed dignity and joy.

verses.text: I will greatly rejoice in the Lord, my soul shall be joyful in my God; for he hath clothed me with the garments of salvation, he hath covered me with the robe of righteousness, as a bridegroom decketh himself with ornaments, and as a bride adorneth herself with her jewels.

For as the earth bringeth forth her bud, and as the garden causeth the things that are sown in it to spring forth; so the Lord God will cause righteousness and praise to spring forth before all the nations.

segments.text: The speaker rejoices as if dressed for a wedding. Clothing pictures salvation and righteousness received through God's care. A garden is another image of growth: righteousness and praise spring up like living plants. These pictures connect the opening mission of healing and comfort with a joyful response. The lesson invites us to notice how the Savior's work can bring hope into places of grief.

Chapter summary. Isaiah sixty-one announces a mission of good news, healing, freedom, and comfort. Jesus later identified this prophecy with His own work. The chapter pictures ruined communities being restored, families receiving lasting blessings, and God's people rejoicing in His salvation. Here are four takeaways. First, learn to recognize Jesus Christ through the care He offers to people who suffer. Second, remember that grief and discouragement belong within the reach of His compassion. Third, join worship with honest and fair actions. Fourth, look for signs of new growth as you turn toward God. A small application is to comfort someone without rushing them, offer practical help, or remember a way the Savior has given you hope. The chapter's images of changed clothing and a growing garden invite us to expect renewal through Him.

chapters.title: Isaiah 62
chapters.focus: God's faithful love, light, and gathering

segments.text: This study reading covers Isaiah chapter sixty-two, with generated explanations for beginners. Isaiah describes God's continuing commitment to Zion through images of light, new names, and a prepared path home.

verses.text: For Zion’s sake will I not hold my peace, and for Jerusalem’s sake I will not rest, until the righteousness thereof go forth as brightness, and the salvation thereof as a lamp that burneth.
And the Gentiles shall see thy righteousness, and all kings thy glory: and thou shalt be called by a new name, which the mouth of the Lord shall name.
Thou shalt also be a crown of glory in the hand of the Lord, and a royal diadem in the hand of thy God.

Thou shalt no more be termed Forsaken; neither shall thy land any more be termed Desolate: but thou shalt be called Hephzi-bah, and thy land Beulah: for the Lord delighteth in thee, and thy land shall be married.
For as a young man marrieth a virgin, so shall thy sons marry thee: and as the bridegroom rejoiceth over the bride, so shall thy God rejoice over thee.

segments.text: The city is described as precious to God. A diadem is a royal crown. The unfamiliar names in verse four express God's delight in His people and a restored relationship pictured as marriage. A bridegroom is a man at his wedding. That joy helps us picture God's love for a community that once felt abandoned. The new names announce a new identity and future.

verses.text: I have set watchmen upon thy walls, O Jerusalem, which shall never hold their peace day nor night: ye that make mention of the Lord, keep not silence,
And give him no rest, till he establish, and till he make Jerusalem a praise in the earth.

The Lord hath sworn by his right hand, and by the arm of his strength, Surely I will no more give thy corn to be meat for thine enemies; and the sons of the stranger shall not drink thy wine, for the which thou hast laboured:
But they that have gathered it shall eat it, and praise the Lord; and they that have brought it together shall drink it in the courts of my holiness.

segments.text: Watchmen were guards who stayed alert on a city's walls. Here their steady calling also pictures prayer and concern for Jerusalem's restoration. The promise about food means people will enjoy what they have worked to grow instead of losing it to enemies. Corn is an older word for grain here. The passage joins faithful waiting and prayer with hope for a secure life.

verses.text: Go through, go through the gates; prepare ye the way of the people; cast up, cast up the highway; gather out the stones; lift up a standard for the people.
Behold, the Lord hath proclaimed unto the end of the world, Say ye to the daughter of Zion, Behold, thy salvation cometh; behold, his reward is with him, and his work before him.
And they shall call them, The holy people, The redeemed of the Lord: and thou shalt be called, Sought out, A city not forsaken.

segments.text: A standard is a raised banner people can gather around. Clearing stones from the highway pictures preparing a route so people can come home. The daughter of Zion is a way of addressing the city and its people. The Redeemer gives them a new description: sought out and cared for. We can reflect on how our actions make another person's path toward God more welcoming.

Chapter summary. Isaiah sixty-two pictures God's people receiving light, honor, and a renewed relationship with Him. Watchmen continue to call for restoration, and the highway is prepared for the people's return. The chapter ends with a community known as redeemed and sought out. Here are four takeaways. First, remember the value God places on His people. Second, bring your hopes and concerns to Him in prayer. Third, help remove obstacles for someone trying to draw closer to God. Fourth, let His faithful love influence the way you describe yourself and others. A small application is to welcome someone who feels overlooked, answer a question patiently, or make a place where someone can belong. The cleared road gives us a practical image of helping people find their way home.

chapters.title: Isaiah 63
chapters.focus: The Redeemer's justice, compassion, and faithful care

segments.text: This study reading covers Isaiah chapter sixty-three, with generated explanations for beginners. The chapter moves from a powerful image of judgment to memories of God's kindness and a heartfelt prayer for His help.

verses.text: Who is this that cometh from Edom, with dyed garments from Bozrah? this that is glorious in his apparel, travelling in the greatness of his strength? I that speak in righteousness, mighty to save.
Wherefore art thou red in thine apparel, and thy garments like him that treadeth in the winefat?

I have trodden the winepress alone; and of the people there was none with me: for I will tread them in mine anger, and trample them in my fury; and their blood shall be sprinkled upon my garments, and I will stain all my raiment.
For the day of vengeance is in mine heart, and the year of my redeemed is come.
And I looked, and there was none to help; and I wondered that there was none to uphold: therefore mine own arm brought salvation unto me; and my fury, it upheld me.
And I will tread down the people in mine anger, and make them drunk in my fury, and I will bring down their strength to the earth.

segments.text: A winepress was used to crush grapes, staining the worker's clothing with juice. Isaiah uses that strong red-clothing image to describe God's judgment against evil. Edom and Bozrah name an enemy land and one of its cities in the picture. Doctrine and Covenants section one hundred thirty-three uses the same imagery for the Savior's return. Notice the speaker's identity: He is mighty to save.

verses.text: I will mention the lovingkindnesses of the Lord, and the praises of the Lord, according to all that the Lord hath bestowed on us, and the great goodness toward the house of Israel, which he hath bestowed on them according to his mercies, and according to the multitude of his lovingkindnesses.
For he said, Surely they are my people, children that will not lie: so he was their Saviour.
In all their affliction he was afflicted, and the angel of his presence saved them: in his love and in his pity he redeemed them; and he bare them, and carried them all the days of old.

segments.text: Lovingkindness means faithful, compassionate care. The tone changes as the speaker remembers God's goodness. Verse nine describes the Lord sharing His people's suffering and carrying them in love. The lesson asks us to notice these descriptions of the Savior. Remembering His compassion helps us see His character alongside the chapter's earlier image of judgment.

verses.text: But they rebelled, and vexed his holy Spirit: therefore he was turned to be their enemy, and he fought against them.
Then he remembered the days of old, Moses, and his people, saying, Where is he that brought them up out of the sea with the shepherd of his flock? where is he that put his holy Spirit within him?
That led them by the right hand of Moses with his glorious arm, dividing the water before them, to make himself an everlasting name?
That led them through the deep, as an horse in the wilderness, that they should not stumble?
As a beast goeth down into the valley, the Spirit of the Lord caused him to rest: so didst thou lead thy people, to make thyself a glorious name.

segments.text: Moses was the prophet who led the Israelites out of Egypt. The sea being divided recalls their escape from slavery. The community remembers both its rebellion and the Lord's earlier deliverance. The gentle picture of an animal resting in a valley contrasts with danger during the journey. Recalling God's past help gives this prayer a reason to hope for help again.

verses.text: Look down from heaven, and behold from the habitation of thy holiness and of thy glory: where is thy zeal and thy strength, the sounding of thy bowels and of thy mercies toward me? are they restrained?
Doubtless thou art our father, though Abraham be ignorant of us, and Israel acknowledge us not: thou, O Lord, art our father, our redeemer; thy name is from everlasting.
O Lord, why hast thou made us to err from thy ways, and hardened our heart from thy fear? Return for thy servants’ sake, the tribes of thine inheritance.
The people of thy holiness have possessed it but a little while: our adversaries have trodden down thy sanctuary.
We are thine: thou never barest rule over them; they were not called by thy name.

segments.text: The people now speak directly to God as their Father and Redeemer. The sounding of thy bowels is an old expression connected with deep inward feeling and compassion. They are distressed because their holy place has been trampled and God feels distant. This is a lament, a prayer that brings grief and difficult questions to Him. It continues into the next chapter as a plea for His presence and mercy.

Chapter summary. Isaiah sixty-three shows the Redeemer confronting evil, then turns to His loving care for His people. Memories of deliverance through Moses lead into a prayer from a suffering community. The Lord is described both as mighty to save and as compassionate toward people in pain. Here are four takeaways. First, take God's concern for justice seriously. Second, remember the kindness and help He has already given. Third, look to the Savior's compassion when you are hurting. Fourth, bring honest sorrow and questions to Him in prayer. A small application is to write down one way you have received help, or thank someone whose kindness made a difficult time easier. Remembering care received can give you something concrete to hold onto while seeking God's help again.

chapters.title: Isaiah 64
chapters.focus: Seeking God's presence and preparing for Christ's return

sources.title: Russell M. Nelson: The Future of the Church (April 2020)

segments.text: This study reading covers Isaiah chapter sixty-four, with generated explanations for beginners. It continues the prayer from the previous chapter, asking God to come near and restore His people.

verses.text: Oh that thou wouldest rend the heavens, that thou wouldest come down, that the mountains might flow down at thy presence,
As when the melting fire burneth, the fire causeth the waters to boil, to make thy name known to thine adversaries, that the nations may tremble at thy presence!
When thou didst terrible things which we looked not for, thou camest down, the mountains flowed down at thy presence.
For since the beginning of the world men have not heard, nor perceived by the ear, neither hath the eye seen, O God, beside thee, what he hath prepared for him that waiteth for him.
Thou meetest him that rejoiceth and worketh righteousness, those that remember thee in thy ways: behold, thou art wroth; for we have sinned: in those is continuance, and we shall be saved.

segments.text: Rend means tear open. The people long for heaven to open and for God to come with unmistakable power. Mountains, fire, and boiling water picture how overwhelming His presence can be. Terrible here can mean awe-inspiring or fearsome. The prayer also remembers that He meets people who do what is right. The lesson connects this longing with preparing for the Savior's coming.

verses.text: But we are all as an unclean thing, and all our righteousnesses are as filthy rags; and we all do fade as a leaf; and our iniquities, like the wind, have taken us away.
And there is none that calleth upon thy name, that stirreth up himself to take hold of thee: for thou hast hid thy face from us, and hast consumed us, because of our iniquities.

segments.text: The community admits its sins. Fading leaves and wind picture how wrongdoing has left the people vulnerable and scattered. The language about filthy rags expresses their need for cleansing and help. This confession belongs within a prayer to God: they recognize the harm and seek a restored relationship. In the next verses, notice the hopeful name they still use for Him.

verses.text: But now, O Lord, thou art our father; we are the clay, and thou our potter; and we all are the work of thy hand.
Be not wroth very sore, O Lord, neither remember iniquity for ever: behold, see, we beseech thee, we are all thy people.

segments.text: A potter shapes clay into something useful. The people call God their Father and compare themselves to clay in His hands. Even while admitting wrongdoing, they remember that they belong to Him and ask for mercy. This image invites us to be willing to change. Repentance means turning away from wrong choices and turning toward God, trusting Him to help shape our lives.

verses.text: Thy holy cities are a wilderness, Zion is a wilderness, Jerusalem a desolation.
Our holy and our beautiful house, where our fathers praised thee, is burned up with fire: and all our pleasant things are laid waste.
Wilt thou refrain thyself for these things, O Lord? wilt thou hold thy peace, and afflict us very sore?

segments.text: The prayer ends by naming ruined cities and a burned holy house, a place of worship. The people ask for God's help in their devastation. The lesson links this chapter with Christ's future return. In his linked message about preparing the world for that day, President Russell M Nelson encourages strengthening faith in Jesus Christ and participating in His work now. Waiting can include faithful choices, learning, and service.

Chapter summary. Isaiah sixty-four is a prayer for God's presence, forgiveness, and restoration. The people remember His power, admit their need for help, and call Him their Father. The potter and clay picture a relationship in which God can shape them as they turn toward Him. Here are four takeaways. First, bring your need for help to God in prayer. Second, be honest about choices that need to change. Third, remember that asking for mercy goes with being willing to learn and grow. Fourth, prepare for the Savior through faithful actions today. A small application is to choose one habit that helps you become more teachable, such as listening carefully, praying sincerely, or making a needed apology. Let the picture of clay in the potter's hands remind you that growth can continue.

chapters.title: Isaiah 65
chapters.focus: Responding to God and hoping for the Savior's reign of peace

segments.text: This study reading covers Isaiah chapter sixty-five, with generated explanations for beginners. God answers the people's prayer by addressing their choices and describing a future of renewed life and peace.

verses.text: I am sought of them that asked not for me; I am found of them that sought me not: I said, Behold me, behold me, unto a nation that was not called by my name.
I have spread out my hands all the day unto a rebellious people, which walketh in a way that was not good, after their own thoughts;
A people that provoketh me to anger continually to my face; that sacrificeth in gardens, and burneth incense upon altars of brick;
Which remain among the graves, and lodge in the monuments, which eat swine’s flesh, and broth of abominable things is in their vessels;
Which say, Stand by thyself, come not near to me; for I am holier than thou. These are a smoke in my nose, a fire that burneth all the day.
Behold, it is written before me: I will not keep silence, but will recompense, even recompense into their bosom,

Your iniquities, and the iniquities of your fathers together, saith the Lord, which have burned incense upon the mountains, and blasphemed me upon the hills: therefore will I measure their former work into their bosom.

segments.text: God describes Himself holding out His hands to people who keep turning away. The forbidden foods and worship practices belong to the setting of ancient Israel's law and worship. Notice the attitude in verse five: people claim to be holier than others while ignoring God's direction. Isaiah's warning challenges both rebellion and pride. The invitation to respond to God stands beside the seriousness of refusing Him.

verses.text: Thus saith the Lord, As the new wine is found in the cluster, and one saith, Destroy it not; for a blessing is in it: so will I do for my servants’ sakes, that I may not destroy them all.
And I will bring forth a seed out of Jacob, and out of Judah an inheritor of my mountains: and mine elect shall inherit it, and my servants shall dwell there.
And Sharon shall be a fold of flocks, and the valley of Achor a place for the herds to lie down in, for my people that have sought me.

segments.text: A cluster of grapes still containing good fruit pictures something worth preserving. God promises to preserve His servants rather than treat everyone as the same. Seed means descendants. Flocks and herds in safe pastures picture a restored home and a secure future. The chapter's warnings are followed by a promise of care for people who seek the Lord.

verses.text: But ye are they that forsake the Lord, that forget my holy mountain, that prepare a table for that troop, and that furnish the drink offering unto that number.

Therefore will I number you to the sword, and ye shall all bow down to the slaughter: because when I called, ye did not answer; when I spake, ye did not hear; but did evil before mine eyes, and did choose that wherein I delighted not.

Therefore thus saith the Lord God, Behold, my servants shall eat, but ye shall be hungry: behold, my servants shall drink, but ye shall be thirsty: behold, my servants shall rejoice, but ye shall be ashamed:
Behold, my servants shall sing for joy of heart, but ye shall cry for sorrow of heart, and shall howl for vexation of spirit.
And ye shall leave your name for a curse unto my chosen: for the Lord God shall slay thee, and call his servants by another name:

That he who blesseth himself in the earth shall bless himself in the God of truth; and he that sweareth in the earth shall swear by the God of truth; because the former troubles are forgotten, and because they are hid from mine eyes.

segments.text: The contrast between eating and hunger, joy and sorrow, shows two different responses to God leading to different outcomes. The central issue is that people were called but would not listen. The God of truth is the one in whom His servants place their trust. As former troubles fade from view, the passage prepares us for the larger promise of a renewed creation.

verses.text: For, behold, I create new heavens and a new earth: and the former shall not be remembered, nor come into mind.
But be ye glad and rejoice for ever in that which I create: for, behold, I create Jerusalem a rejoicing, and her people a joy.
And I will rejoice in Jerusalem, and joy in my people: and the voice of weeping shall be no more heard in her, nor the voice of crying.

segments.text: New heavens and a new earth picture God's renewal of the world. Jerusalem becomes a place of joy rather than weeping. The lesson points to the Savior's future reign. In Church teaching, the Millennium is the thousand-year period of peace when Jesus Christ reigns after His Second Coming. These verses help us imagine why His coming can be a source of hope and rejoicing.

verses.text: There shall be no more thence an infant of days, nor an old man that hath not filled his days: for the child shall die an hundred years old; but the sinner being an hundred years old shall be accursed.
And they shall build houses, and inhabit them; and they shall plant vineyards, and eat the fruit of them.
They shall not build, and another inhabit; they shall not plant, and another eat: for as the days of a tree are the days of my people, and mine elect shall long enjoy the work of their hands.
They shall not labour in vain, nor bring forth for trouble; for they are the seed of the blessed of the Lord, and their offspring with them.
And it shall come to pass, that before they call, I will answer; and while they are yet speaking, I will hear.

The wolf and the lamb shall feed together, and the lion shall eat straw like the bullock: and dust shall be the serpent’s meat. They shall not hurt nor destroy in all my holy mountain, saith the Lord.

segments.text: An infant of days means a baby whose life lasts only a few days. Isaiah contrasts such loss with long, full lives. Houses, gardens, and work that benefits the people doing it picture security. Even natural enemies are shown living peacefully together. The tenth Article of Faith teaches that Christ will reign personally on earth and that the earth will be renewed. The images here help us look toward that promised peace.

Chapter summary. Isaiah sixty-five calls people to respond to God honestly and humbly. It warns about stubborn refusal and pride, then promises preservation and a renewed future for His people. The final picture includes joy, secure homes, fruitful work, and peace across creation. Here are four takeaways. First, listen for God's direction instead of simply defending your own choices. Second, treat other people with humility rather than declaring yourself better than they are. Third, let the Savior's promised future strengthen your hope. Fourth, practice the kind of peace and care you look forward to in His reign. A small application is to help make a home, classroom, or conversation more peaceful. Isaiah's future picture can shape the way we live with other people today.

chapters.title: Isaiah 66
chapters.focus: Humble worship, divine comfort, and the gathering of all nations

segments.text: This study reading covers Isaiah chapter sixty-six, with generated explanations for beginners. The final chapter brings together humble worship, God's comfort, the seriousness of judgment, and the gathering of people from many nations.

verses.text: Thus saith the Lord, The heaven is my throne, and the earth is my footstool: where is the house that ye build unto me? and where is the place of my rest?
For all those things hath mine hand made, and all those things have been, saith the Lord: but to this man will I look, even to him that is poor and of a contrite spirit, and trembleth at my word.

He that killeth an ox is as if he slew a man; he that sacrificeth a lamb, as if he cut off a dog’s neck; he that offereth an oblation, as if he offered swine’s blood; he that burneth incense, as if he blessed an idol. Yea, they have chosen their own ways, and their soul delighteth in their abominations.

I also will choose their delusions, and will bring their fears upon them; because when I called, none did answer; when I spake, they did not hear: but they did evil before mine eyes, and chose that in which I delighted not.

segments.text: God begins as Creator of heaven and earth, then points to the heart of the worshipper. Contrite means sincerely sorry for wrongdoing and willing to change. Trembling at His word pictures taking Him seriously. The severe comparisons between sacrifices and offensive actions expose worship joined with disobedience. The question is what kind of heart we bring when we offer our worship.

verses.text: Hear the word of the Lord, ye that tremble at his word; Your brethren that hated you, that cast you out for my name’s sake, said, Let the Lord be glorified: but he shall appear to your joy, and they shall be ashamed.
A voice of noise from the city, a voice from the temple, a voice of the Lord that rendereth recompence to his enemies.
Before she travailed, she brought forth; before her pain came, she was delivered of a man child.

Who hath heard such a thing? who hath seen such things? Shall the earth be made to bring forth in one day? or shall a nation be born at once? for as soon as Zion travailed, she brought forth her children.
Shall I bring to the birth, and not cause to bring forth? saith the Lord: shall I cause to bring forth, and shut the womb? saith thy God.

segments.text: Some faithful people are being rejected by others. God promises that the outcome will bring them joy. The chapter then pictures Zion like a mother giving birth, with a new community appearing surprisingly quickly. Travail means the struggle and pain of childbirth. The image emphasizes God's power to bring His purposes to fulfillment and give new life to His people.

verses.text: Rejoice ye with Jerusalem, and be glad with her, all ye that love her: rejoice for joy with her, all ye that mourn for her:
That ye may suck, and be satisfied with the breasts of her consolations; that ye may milk out, and be delighted with the abundance of her glory.

For thus saith the Lord, Behold, I will extend peace to her like a river, and the glory of the Gentiles like a flowing stream: then shall ye suck, ye shall be borne upon her sides, and be dandled upon her knees.
As one whom his mother comforteth, so will I comfort you; and ye shall be comforted in Jerusalem.
And when ye see this, your heart shall rejoice, and your bones shall flourish like an herb: and the hand of the Lord shall be known toward his servants, and his indignation toward his enemies.

segments.text: Jerusalem is pictured as a mother who nourishes and comforts her children. Dandled upon her knees means being lovingly held and bounced, as a caregiver might hold a small child. Peace flows like a river. The Lord uses a mother's comforting care to help us imagine His own compassion. Notice the invitation to rejoice with people whose sorrow is being replaced by hope.

verses.text: For, behold, the Lord will come with fire, and with his chariots like a whirlwind, to render his anger with fury, and his rebuke with flames of fire.
For by fire and by his sword will the Lord plead with all flesh: and the slain of the Lord shall be many.
They that sanctify themselves, and purify themselves in the gardens behind one tree in the midst, eating swine’s flesh, and the abomination, and the mouse, shall be consumed together, saith the Lord.

segments.text: Fire, a whirlwind, and a sword picture the force and seriousness of God's judgment. The references to forbidden foods and worship in gardens describe practices condemned in ancient Israel's setting. The lesson places these chapters within the hope of Christ's coming reign. That hope includes God's response to evil as well as His comfort and peace for His people.

verses.text: For I know their works and their thoughts: it shall come, that I will gather all nations and tongues; and they shall come, and see my glory.

And I will set a sign among them, and I will send those that escape of them unto the nations, to Tarshish, Pul, and Lud, that draw the bow, to Tubal, and Javan, to the isles afar off, that have not heard my fame, neither have seen my glory; and they shall declare my glory among the Gentiles.

And they shall bring all your brethren for an offering unto the Lord out of all nations upon horses, and in chariots, and in litters, and upon mules, and upon swift beasts, to my holy mountain Jerusalem, saith the Lord, as the children of Israel bring an offering in a clean vessel into the house of the Lord.
And I will also take of them for priests and for Levites, saith the Lord.
For as the new heavens and the new earth, which I will make, shall remain before me, saith the Lord, so shall your seed and your name remain.
And it shall come to pass, that from one new moon to another, and from one sabbath to another, shall all flesh come to worship before me, saith the Lord.

And they shall go forth, and look upon the carcases of the men that have transgressed against me: for their worm shall not die, neither shall their fire be quenched; and they shall be an abhorring unto all flesh.

segments.text: Tongues means languages. The gathering reaches many peoples and faraway places, and those who know the Lord share His glory with others. Levites were members of a tribe associated with service in ancient Israel's worship. The chapter promises continuing worship in God's renewed creation, then closes with a stark image of judgment. The contrast leaves us with an important choice: receive God's invitation with humility and live in response to Him.

Chapter summary. Isaiah sixty-six begins with humble hearts taking God's word seriously. It pictures the restoration of Zion, tender comfort, and peace, while also warning about judgment. Its vision reaches across nations and languages as people gather to worship the Lord. Here are four takeaways. First, bring a teachable and repentant heart to worship. Second, remember the tenderness in God's care when you need comfort. Third, join His work by welcoming and helping people beyond your familiar circle. Fourth, let the hope of His renewed world encourage faithful choices now. A small application is to listen respectfully to someone, comfort a person who is struggling, or make a sincere change in your own behavior. These final chapters invite us to know the Redeemer through both His mighty power and His compassionate love.
